lead: Joseph’s story moves from plot to deed: he is stripped, thrown into a pit and sold, and his father is left in grief. In John, some Greeks ask to see Jesus, and he answers that the hour has come and speaks of a grain of wheat that must die. Both readings say that what looks like an end is the way God brings fruit. Between them, Joshua 22:30–23:1 shows brothers who listen before they fight, and peace is restored, the very thing Joseph’s brothers would not do. Hebrews 5:1–10 names the Son who “learned obedience through what he suffered” (5:8).

r.h: Sold for twenty pieces of silver
set: The plan of vv. 18–22 is carried out, but not as anyone intended. Reuben meant to rescue Joseph; Judah proposes the sale; Jacob is deceived with a robe dipped in blood, as he once deceived his own father with goatskin (27:16).

The chapter speaks of both Ishmaelites and Midianites as the traders (vv. 25, 28, 36). Many scholars think two forms of the story have been joined here. What the text says clearly is that Joseph’s own brothers bear the guilt: Joseph later says to them, “whom you sold into Egypt” (45:4).
str: vv. 23–24: the robe and the pit.
vv. 25–28: the brothers eat; a caravan passes; Judah’s proposal; the sale.
vv. 29–30: Reuben finds the pit empty.
vv. 31–35: the robe in goat’s blood; Jacob’s mourning.
v. 36: Joseph is sold on to Potiphar. God has not been named once, yet the story is moving.
kw: The exact meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The old “coat of many colours” comes from the Greek and Latin translations. It is a garment of honour, and 2 Samuel 13:18 uses the same words for a king’s daughter’s robe.
An empty cistern cut in rock for rainwater. The same word is used for the grave in the Psalms (for example Psalm 88:4). Joseph goes down, as if alive into the place of the dead.
The brothers’ words to Jacob over the robe (v. 32). Tamar will use the same words to Judah in the next chapter (38:25). The man who deceived is himself brought to the truth.
vv: The pit was empty; there was no water in it.
A small detail that means slow death. Zechariah speaks of prisoners in a “waterless pit” (9:11), a passage read on Hosanna Sunday.
Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and not lay our hands on him, for he is our brother, our own flesh.
Judah’s words sound like mercy, but they make a profit out of a brother. Judah and Judas are the same name, and Christian readers have noticed the link between this sale and the one Judas makes.
sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver.
Twenty shekels is the value Leviticus 27:5 sets on a male between five and twenty years old. Thirty was the compensation for a slave (Exodus 21:32), the sum paid to Judas (Matthew 26:15).
All his sons and all his daughters sought to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted,
Those comforting him know what he does not know. Genesis does not hurry past a father’s grief, and this week neither should we.
ch: Psalm 105 sings: “he had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave” (105:17). Nothing in the sale was good, and yet God was “sending” him. Joseph says it himself at the end: “Even though you intended to do harm to me, God intended it for good” (50:20). The Catechism uses this as its example of providence (CCC 312). The Fathers saw Christ here: St Ambrose, among others, sees in Joseph the one who was stripped and sold and who became the saviour of those who sold him (in substance).

set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem to the crowd’s cry of Hosanna (12:12–19). Now some “Greeks” come to worship at the festival. They are probably people of Gentile birth drawn to the God of Israel. They approach Philip, who has a Greek name and comes from Bethsaida, a town on the edge of Greek-speaking territory. That the nations are now coming is the signal Jesus has been waiting for.
Up to now the hour has “not yet come” (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now he says it has come.
str: vv. 20–22: the request passes from the Greeks to Philip, to Andrew, to Jesus.
vv. 25–26: what this means for the disciple.
kw: In John, the hour is the time of the Cross and of the return to the Father together. For John, the Cross is already glory.
A single seed. The POC says it must decay in the ground (അഴിയുക), where the Greek says “die”. Either way it is the only road to harvest.

Semitic speech uses “love” and “hate” to mean “put first” and “put second” (compare Luke 14:26 with Matthew 10:37). Jesus is not teaching contempt for the life God has given; he is teaching what comes first.
vv: Sir, we wish to see Jesus.
It is a good prayer for anyone. They are not told that they saw him. Jesus’ answer tells them where he will be seen: lifted up.
Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
Jesus says this first about himself. The Greeks and all the nations will come to him through his death and not around it.
Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.
Where he is this week is the Cross. And where he is after that is with the Father. The promise covers both.
ch: St Augustine reads the grain as Christ himself, who dies and is multiplied in the faith of the nations (in substance). St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom, applied the image to himself: he called himself God’s wheat, to be ground by the teeth of beasts so as to become the pure bread of Christ (Letter to the Romans 4, in substance). The grain is thus also a word about the Holy Qurbana, where wheat becomes the bread of life.

study: Joseph’s brothers sat down to eat beside the pit. Where do I sit comfortably near someone else’s suffering?
What in my life is the Lord asking me to let “fall into the earth” this week, so that it may bear fruit?
